1.meaning: A combined opener meaning roughly 'Have ... not ...?' — it fuses the question-word 'a (Did/Have?) with lam (not), turning the verb that follows into a negated question. Here it does not expect the answer 'no'; it is a gentle rhetorical question inviting the listener to affirm 'Yes, You certainly did,' as Allah reminds the Prophet of a favour already granted.

parts.en: a negating particle: 'not' (placed before a present-tense verb to turn it into a completed past negative)

1.grammar: Two particles fused into one. The opening 'a- asks a question; lam is a negator that does a special job: it takes a present-tense verb form and pushes its meaning into the past, while also putting that verb into the 'jussive' mood (which is why the next word ends in a bare, vowel-less form). Together 'a-lam means 'Did it not happen that...?' — a question whose expected answer is a confident 'yes, it did.'

2.meaning: 'We opened up / expanded / made spacious.' The image is of widening the chest so it becomes roomy and at ease — opening the Prophet's heart to receive revelation, wisdom and tranquillity, and lifting anxiety from it.
2.grammar: A present-tense verb. The na- prefix at the front means the doer is 'we' (the majestic 'We' of Allah). Although the form is present-tense in shape, it is governed by the preceding lam, so its sense is past: 'We expanded.' That governing also strips the ending bare — note the final vowel-less -ḥ (nashraḥ, not nashraḥu) — which is the mark of the jussive mood demanded by lam.
2.root: ش-ر-ح (sh-r-ḥ) — to open, lay open, expand the chest

3.meaning: 'For you' / 'to you' — singling out the Prophet as the one for whose benefit this opening was done. The phrasing highlights that the favour was specially for him.
3.grammar: A preposition plus an attached pronoun. la- means 'for/to' and carries the sense of something done for one's benefit. The ending -ka is the attached pronoun 'you' (one male person), in the object form that always follows a preposition. So laka = 'for you,' emphasising that the Prophet personally is the recipient.

4.meaning: 'Your breast / chest' — understood as the seat of the heart, feelings and inner state. To open someone's 'breast' is to broaden their capacity, calm their distress, and make them receptive to truth.

parts.en: 'breast / chest' (the inner self, the heart's seat)

4.grammar: A noun with an attached possessive pronoun. ṣadr means 'breast/chest'; the final -ka means 'your' (one male), so the word means 'your breast.' The -a vowel before the pronoun (ṣadra-) is the accusative (object) ending: it marks this word as the thing being acted upon — i.e. the breast is what 'We opened.'
4.root: ص-د-ر (ṣ-d-r) — chest, breast; the front or foremost part

1.meaning: And We removed / set aside — Allah declares that He took away and laid aside a weight that had been pressing on the Prophet. The verb is one of setting down and putting away, not lifting up; the load was set off the Prophet rather than raised. The 'We' is the royal 'We' of divine majesty, not plurality.

parts.en: and (connector joining this to the previous favour)

1.grammar: A past-tense verb. The attached -nā ending means 'we' as the subject — the act is finished and completed ('We removed'). It carries the majestic plural of Allah. The verb governs what follows: it removed something (wizr) from someone (ʿanka).
1.root: و-ض-ع (w-ḍ-ʿ) — to put down, set down, lay aside, set away. In this verse the sense is that the burden was laid away from the Prophet (removed from him), not pushed downward; it is the opposite of رَفَعَ (to lift / raise up) used in 94:4.

2.meaning: Off you / away from you — a preposition fused with 'you', marking the person from whom the burden was taken away. It conveys removal and separation: the load was set off the Prophet's person.
2.grammar: A preposition ('off / away from') with an attached pronoun. The -ka ending is the object of the preposition and means 'you' (one man). Together with the verb, it shows the burden was removed from 'you' specifically — the Prophet.
2.root: — (ʿan is a preposition / particle and has no triliteral root; the suffix -ka is a pronoun)

3.meaning: Your burden — a heavy load or weight, here the grief and crushing responsibility carried by the Prophet (understood by commentators as the strain of his mission and the cares that weighed on his heart).
3.grammar: A noun with an attached possessive pronoun. The -a on wizr- is the accusative ending: it marks this word as the direct object — the thing that was removed. The final -ka means 'your' (one man), showing the burden belonged to the Prophet.
3.root: و-ز-ر (w-z-r) — to bear a heavy load; a burden or weight (also the sense behind 'wazīr', one who carries the load of office)

1.meaning: A relative pronoun meaning 'the one which / that which.' It points back to the burden mentioned in the previous verse and introduces a description of it. In English we render it simply as 'which' or 'that.'

parts.en: the (definite element of the relative pronoun)

1.grammar: This is the masculine singular relative pronoun ('the one which'). It is invariable here — it does not change for case — and it agrees in gender and number with the masculine singular noun it describes (the burden, wizr, from verse 2). The long final -ī simply belongs to the fixed form of the word; it is not a case ending. Its job is to hook the following clause ('weighed down your back') onto that noun.

2.meaning: It weighed down heavily, pressed down with a crushing load — so much so that it made a cracking or creaking sound, the way an overloaded back or beam groans under strain. The image is of a weight that nearly breaks what it rests on.

parts.en: it weighed down / made (something) crack and strain under a load

2.grammar: This is a past-tense (perfect) verb, third person masculine singular: 'it weighed down.' The final -a with no attached subject pronoun is the default 'he/it (did)' form. It is built on the triliteral root n-q-ḍ (ن-ق-ض) in Form IV — the أَفْعَلَ (afʿala) pattern, which here carries a causative sense, 'to cause to crack or groan under a load.' In this pattern the opening hamza (the اَ) is part of the verb's own shape, not a detachable prefix bolted onto a separate base verb, and all three radicals n-q-ḍ are present (the ن is the first root letter). Its hidden subject 'it' refers back to the burden; the next word is its object.
2.root: ن-ق-ض (n-q-ḍ) — to break apart, undo, or make a cracking/creaking sound under strain

3.meaning: Your back — the upper back and spine, pictured here as the part of the body that bears a heavy load. By extension it evokes the weight of responsibility and hardship pressing down on the Prophet.
3.grammar: A noun, 'back,' with the attached pronoun -ka ('your,' to one male — the Prophet). The -a vowel before that pronoun is the accusative case ending, which marks this word as the direct object of the verb: it is the thing that was weighed down. The suffix -ka shows possession ('your back').
3.root: ظ-ه-ر (ẓ-h-r) — the back; also to appear, become manifest, or be uppermost

1.meaning: "And We raised high / elevated." Allah declares that He lifted up and exalted something belonging to the Prophet — here, his renown. The opening "And" links this favour to the previous ones (expanding his breast, lifting his burden). The "We" is the royal/majestic plural Allah uses of Himself, signalling power and grandeur, not plurality.
1.grammar: A past-tense verb. The attached ending -nā ("we") is the subject: "We raised." It refers to Allah in the majestic plural. The verb is in the simple past, so the act of elevating is presented as already accomplished and certain. The leading wa- is the connector "and," joining this favour to the list before it.

2.meaning: "For you" — that is, for your benefit and in your honour. It singles out the Prophet as the one for whose sake this elevation was done, underscoring that the favour was granted specifically to him.
2.grammar: A preposition la- ("for/to") fused with the attached pronoun -ka ("you"). The -ka ending is the masculine singular "you," addressing the Prophet directly. Placed before the object, the phrase "for you" gives a sense of "it is for your sake" that We did this.

3.meaning: "Your mention / your remembrance." Dhikr is a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning the very act of calling someone to mind and speaking of them — so "your dhikr" is "the mentioning of you," not merely an abstract "fame." Allah raising it means the Prophet's name is invoked and proclaimed everywhere, paired with Allah's own (as in the call to prayer and the testimony of faith).

parts.en: mention / remembrance (the act of mentioning) — verbal noun
accusative case ending (marks it as the object)

3.grammar: A verbal noun (maṣdar) ذِكۡر ("the act of mentioning/remembering") with the attached possessive pronoun -ka ("your"). It is the object of the verb "raised," so it takes the accusative ending -a (the fathah on the ر) — this -a is a grammatical case marker, not part of the lexical stem, which is simply ذِكۡر (dhikr). The -ka is masculine singular "your," again addressing the Prophet: "We raised the mentioning of you."
3.root: ذ-ك-ر (dh-k-r) — to mention, remember, call to mind

1.meaning: A connector plus an emphatic opener. The fa- links this verse to what came before ('and so', 'therefore'), drawing a conclusion from Allah's favours just mentioned. The inna is a particle of emphasis that has no real English equivalent; it stamps the whole statement as a solemn, certain truth, best felt as 'truly', 'indeed', or 'most surely'.

parts.en: so / and so (connecting to the previous verses)

1.grammar: fa- is a prefixed conjunction meaning 'so/therefore', tying this verse to the favours described before. inna is an emphasis particle that introduces a noun sentence and grammatically puts its subject (the ismu inna) into the accusative case. In this verse that subject is yusran ('ease', word 4), which accordingly carries the accusative ending; it powerfully asserts the certainty of the promise. inna carries no tense or person of its own — it simply guarantees the truth of the sentence.

2.meaning: An adverb of accompaniment meaning 'together with', 'alongside', 'in the company of'. It signals that two things are paired or present at the same time. Here it conveys that ease is not merely after hardship but accompanies it — bound up with it.
2.grammar: maʿa is an adverb of place/accompaniment (zarf) that behaves like a preposition. It governs the word after it, putting 'the hardship' into the genitive case as its muḍāf ilayh (hence the -i ending on al-ʿusri). The fixed final -a is part of the word itself, not a case ending. It stresses togetherness — ease and hardship coexisting, not just succeeding one another.

3.meaning: 'The hardship' — difficulty, distress, strain; the state of finding things hard going. The definite article 'the' is significant: classical scholars note it points to a specific, known hardship (the trials of the Prophet and the believers), and that when this same definite 'the hardship' is repeated in the next verse it refers to the very same single hardship.
3.grammar: A definite noun: al- is 'the', and the stem is ʿusr. The final -i ending is the genitive case, because it is the muḍāf ilayh governed by the preceding adverb maʿa ('with the hardship'). The definite article here is the 'al- of prior knowledge' (al- lil-ʿahd) — it marks a particular, already-known hardship rather than hardship in general.
3.root: ع-س-ر (ʿ-s-r) — difficulty, hardship, being hard or straitened

4.meaning: 'Ease' — relief, facility, things being made smooth and manageable; the opposite of strain. It is left indefinite ('ease', not 'the ease'), which scholars read as opening it up: an unspecified, abundant ease. Since the hardship is repeated as definite (one and the same) but ease appears indefinite in both verses, the classical conclusion is that the single hardship is met with a manifold, more-than-doubled ease.
4.grammar: An indefinite noun. The stem is yusr, and the final tanwīn (the doubled-fatḥa nunation, -an) marks it as accusative and indefinite. It is accusative because it is the ismu inna (the subject inna throws into the accusative). It appears at the very end of the sentence because the predicate, maʿa l-ʿusri ('with the hardship'), has been fronted (khabar muqaddam): an adverbial/prepositional phrase normally must precede when the subject is an indefinite noun, so the indefinite ismu yusran is delayed to the end. The absence of 'the' (indefiniteness) suggests an open, unbounded ease.
4.root: ي-س-ر (y-s-r) — ease, facility, being made easy or smooth

1.meaning: An emphatic opening particle meaning roughly 'Truly' or 'Most certainly.' It is not really translatable as a single English word; its job is to grab the listener and stress that the statement that follows is absolutely true and certain. Here it underscores the divine promise that ease accompanies hardship.
1.grammar: A particle of emphasis and assertion (one of the 'sisters of inna'). It introduces a noun sentence and grammatically puts its subject into the accusative case. It carries no person, tense, or ending of its own to gloss; its whole function is to add the force of 'indeed.' Unlike verse 5 (fa-inna), it appears here without the connector fa- ('so'), so it stands as a fresh, standalone affirmation.

2.meaning: A word meaning 'with,' 'alongside,' or 'in the company of.' It conveys togetherness in time and place — the ease is not merely after the hardship but accompanies it, paired with it.
2.grammar: An adverb of accompaniment that functions like a preposition: it must be followed by a noun in the genitive case, which is why the next word carries an -i ending. The final -a here is its own fixed shape and does not change. It tells you the two things named are joined together.

3.meaning: 'The hardship' — difficulty, distress, or a tight, straitened situation that is hard to bear. The 'al-' ('the') makes it specific: the very hardship already mentioned in the previous verse, not some new one.
3.grammar: A definite noun (marked by the prefix al-, 'the'). Its final -i ending is the genitive case, required because it follows the word maʿa ('with') — so it reads 'with the hardship.' Because al- is repeated identically from verse 5, the classical scholars note it points back to the same single hardship rather than a different one.
3.root: ع-س-ر (ʿ-s-r) — difficulty, hardship, being hard or constrained

4.meaning: 'Ease' — relief, comfort, and things being made smooth and manageable. Coming without 'the,' it reads as ease in an open, unlimited sense, which commentators understand as a manifold, abundant ease.
4.grammar: An indefinite noun (no 'the'); the -an ending (tanwīn, the 'n' sound on the end) marks it as indefinite and in the accusative case. It is the delayed subject of inna, asserting that 'ease' is present. Crucially, unlike 'the hardship,' it lacks al- ('the') in both verses 5 and 6 — signalling that the ease is unspecified and, the scholars say, repeated and multiplied.
4.root: ي-س-ر (y-s-r) — ease, facility, being smooth or easy

1.meaning: A two-part connector meaning roughly "so, when...". The fa- piece links this verse to what came before ("so, in light of all that"), and idha sets up a condition about the future: "whenever / once (a certain thing happens)." It tells you a result will follow once the action in the next word is done.
1.grammar: This is a particle cluster, so it has no case ending to parse. fa- is a connector showing consequence ("so"). idha introduces a real future condition — "when / once X happens" — and it points forward to a paired result; here the result is the command in word 3 ("then strive"). Together they form the "once you... then..." frame of the verse.

2.meaning: "You have finished / become free," i.e. you have completed and emptied yourself of a task — discharged your duties and have free, unoccupied time. The sense is being done with one occupation so as to turn to another.

parts.en: finished / became free, empty (of a task)

2.grammar: This is a past-tense verb. The -ta ending is the attached subject pronoun marking a single male addressee — "you finished." Although the form is past, after idha ("when") it carries a future/conditional sense: "once you have finished." The verb's own vowel pattern (faragha) is the plain Form I, describing the action of becoming free itself.
2.root: ف-ر-غ (f-r-gh) — to be empty, free, unoccupied; to finish a task

3.meaning: A command: "then exert yourself / toil hard." It urges strenuous effort and standing up to labour — classically understood as devoting that freed-up time to worship and earnest striving, putting real exertion into it.

parts.en: then (linking the result to the condition)
toil / exert yourself, labour hard (a command)

3.grammar: The fa- here is the "then" that answers the earlier "when" — it delivers the consequence of the condition. inṣab is a direct order (imperative) aimed at one male addressee, "strive!". Its ending sits on a silent/jussive-style final consonant (-ṣab, no added vowel), which is the normal shape of a command in Form I — telling the person to actually do the exerting.
3.root: ن-ص-ب (n-ṣ-b) — to toil, exert oneself, set up / stand firm with effort

1.meaning: "And to / and towards." A linking word joined to a preposition that points the direction of motion or attention toward something. Here it sets up the goal of the command that follows: it is TO your Lord that all longing should be directed. Placing this phrase first (before the verb) gives it emphasis — 'and to your Lord ˹specifically˺...'
1.grammar: Two pieces: the wa- prefix means 'and', joining this verse to the previous one. ilā is a preposition meaning 'to / toward', and it forces the noun after it (rabbika) into the genitive case — which is why 'Lord' below ends in -i. Putting this prepositional phrase before its verb is deliberate word-order for emphasis and exclusivity ('to your Lord alone').

2.meaning: "Your Lord." Rabb is far richer than 'master' or 'boss': it means the One who creates, owns, sustains, nurtures and brings each thing to its completion — the Lord who cares for you and develops you step by step. The attached 'your' makes it intimate and personal: the very Lord who has been raising and providing for you.
2.grammar: Two pieces: rabb 'Lord' plus the suffix -ka 'your' (addressed to one male — the Prophet ︎). The stem shows the -i ending (rabbi): this genitive case is caused by the preposition ilā before it, so it reads 'to your Lord'. The suffix -ka also means the noun is possessed ('Lord OF you' = 'your Lord').
2.root: ر-ب-ب (r-b-b) — to nurture, sustain, own and bring to completion; hence 'Lord'.

3.meaning: "So turn ˹all˺ your longing and hope ˹to Him˺." A command to direct your deepest desire and yearning toward Allah — to want Him, to set your heart's hope and aspiration on Him alone, eagerly and earnestly, rather than on anyone or anything else.
3.grammar: Two pieces: the fa- prefix means 'so / then', drawing a conclusion from what came before ('since all this is true, then...'). irghab is a command (imperative) addressed to one male: 'turn with desire!'. It is a Form I verb; its starting vowel (the 'i-' of irghab) is just the helping vowel (hamzat al-wasl) that lets the command be pronounced — it drops after the fa-, giving fa-irghab. Paired with ilā ('to') above, raghiba ilā specifically means to turn toward something with eager hope and longing.
3.root: ر-غ-ب (r-gh-b) — to desire, yearn, aspire; with ilā, to turn toward with earnest hope.
